Care Transition Efficiency & Placement Outcome Analytics¶

Exploratory data analysis, metric engineering and findings · UAC care pipeline: CBP custody → HHS care → sponsor placement

This notebook walks through every analytical step in the project brief:

  1. Data loading, cleaning and quality assessment
  2. Care-pipeline modelling and transition-efficiency metrics
  3. Backlog and delay identification
  4. Temporal and pattern analysis (weekday vs Sunday, month-over-month, stagnation)
  5. Outcome-stability analysis
  6. Forecast benchmarking (does ML add value?)
  7. Key findings

The reusable logic lives in src/pipeline_metrics.py and is shared with the Streamlit dashboard so the notebook, paper and app always agree.

Three issues are visible immediately:

  • 450 completely blank rows at the end of the file.
  • The HHS column is read as text because of thousands separators ("2,340").
  • Dates are stored as text ("December 21, 2025") and sorted newest first.

load_data() fixes all three and renames the columns to short, safe names.

Reporting calendar: the source reports Monday–Thursday and Sunday only. Friday has just 2 rows and Saturday none, so a Sunday row follows a 3-day gap. Any "weekend" comparison is therefore really Sunday vs Mon–Thu and must be read with that reporting artefact in mind.

2.1 Do flows reconcile with stocks?¶

A pipeline model assumes Δ load = inflow − outflow. We test this on consecutive-day pairs (gap = 1 day): Δ HHS load vs transfers − discharges, and Δ CBP load vs intake − transfers.

In [6]:
d = add_metrics(df, window=7)
d["year"] = d.date.dt.year
c = d[d.gap_days == 1].copy()
c["dhhs"] = d.hhs_load.diff(); c["dcbp"] = d.cbp_load.diff()
rows = []
for y, g in c.groupby("year"):
    rows.append({"year": y, "pairs": len(g), "HHS corr": g.dhhs.corr(g.hhs_net), "CBP corr": g.dcbp.corr(g.cbp_net),
                 "ΔHHS − (transfers−discharges), mean": (g.dhhs - g.hhs_net).mean()})
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(2)
Out[6]:
year pairs HHS corr CBP corr ΔHHS − (transfers−discharges), mean

1 2024 197 0.80 0.75 12.20
2 2025 183 0.98 0.52 3.02
In [7]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
for a, (y, g) in zip(ax, c.groupby("year")):
    a.scatter(g.hhs_net, g.dhhs, s=10, alpha=.6, color="#3D5A80")
    lim = [min(g.hhs_net.min(), g.dhhs.min()), max(g.hhs_net.max(), g.dhhs.max())]
    a.plot(lim, lim, "r--", lw=1); a.set_title(f"{y}: r = {g.dhhs.corr(g.hhs_net):.2f}")
    a.set_xlabel("transfers − discharges"); a.set_ylabel("Δ HHS load")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("Total intake:", d.intake.sum(), "| total transfers:", d.transfers.sum(), "| total discharges:", d.discharges.sum())

Total intake: 67337.0 | total transfers: 92641.0 | total discharges: 124853.0

Finding. Reconciliation is weak in 2023 (r≈0.46), improves in 2024 (0.80) and is near-perfect in 2025 (0.98). In 2023 the HHS stock grew faster than reported net flows imply, i.e. children appear to have entered HHS care through routes other than the reported CBP transfers (or transfers were under-reported). Also, transfers exceed apprehensions by ~38 %, so "apprehended and placed in CBP custody" is a narrower definition than total CBP intake.

Consequence for the analysis: ratio metrics are valid as process indicators, but cumulative flow sums should not be treated as true stock changes. The project therefore reports a flow-based and a stock-based backlog view side by side.

The series shows a structural break in early 2025: CBP custody and HHS care both collapse within roughly two months and then stay at a much lower level. Every later analysis therefore compares before and after this break rather than pooling across it.

4. Transition-efficiency metrics¶

Metric Definition
Transfer Efficiency Ratio (TER) transfers ÷ CBP custody
Discharge Effectiveness Index (DEI) discharges ÷ HHS care
Pipeline Throughput total exits ÷ total entries (discharges ÷ intake)

pre, post = d[d.date < "2025-02-01"], d[d.date >= "2025-04-01"]
for name, col in [("Transfer efficiency", "transfer_eff"), ("Discharge effectiveness", "discharge_eff")]:
    p = stats.mannwhitneyu(pre[col], post[col]).pvalue
    print(f"{name}: before = {pre[col].mean():.3%}, after = {post[col].mean():.3%}, Mann-Whitney p = {p:.1e}")
print(f"Discharges / reporting day: before = {pre.discharges.mean():.0f}, after = {post.discharges.mean():.0f}")

Transfer efficiency: before = 81.047%, after = 35.892%, Mann-Whitney p = 2.0e-69
Discharge effectiveness: before = 3.104%, after = 0.536%, Mann-Whitney p = 7.0e-87
Discharges / reporting day: before = 241, after = 12

Finding. Through 2023–24 about three-quarters of the children in CBP custody were transferred each reporting day and about 3 % of the HHS population was discharged per day. After the early-2025 break, TER falls to ~36 % and DEI to ~0.5 % (both p < 0.001). Throughput stays above 1× in aggregate, meaning outflows kept pace with inflows, but only because the system was draining its stock, not because the process got faster.

Reading the two views together. The flow view says the system was draining almost continuously; the stock view shows repeated build-ups in 2023–24. They disagree because of the reconciliation gap documented in §2.1. Sustained flow-based imbalance is rare (two short episodes), but four prolonged stagnation periods appear in 2025, each with ~2,000–2,500 children in HHS care and only ~10–17 discharges per day (DEI 0.45–0.71 %).

Delay severity (Little's-law approximation). Implied time in CBP custody is stable at ≈ 1.3 days until Q1 2025, then rises to ≈ 3.2–3.4 days in H2 2025, crossing the 72-hour transfer benchmark. Implied time in HHS care rises from ≈ 29 days (Q1 2023) to ≈ 150–230 days in H2 2025. These are indicative (stock ÷ outflow rate, at very low volumes) but the direction and size of the change are unambiguous.

Finding. Transfers are equally fast on every reporting day (Sunday vs Mon–Thu, p = 0.93), but discharges differ significantly by weekday: Tuesday is the weakest day (≈136 / day) and Thursday and Sunday the strongest (≈206 / day). Because Sunday rows follow a 3-day reporting gap they may contain catch-up activity, so this should be validated with complete Friday/Saturday data before changing staffing.

Finding. Stability was steady at ~77/100 in 2023–24, then collapsed to a low of ~6/100 in April 2025 (the 28-day window spanning the transition) and has only partly recovered (~54 average for 2025, hovering just under the 60 alert line). Eight sudden week-on-week drops of ≥30 % were detected, four of them in H2 2025 where daily volumes are so small (≈10) that a handful of cases moves the percentage.

8. Forecast benchmarking – does ML help?¶

To test whether the pipeline is predictable enough for a model to add value, we forecast discharges 5 reporting days ahead using 5-fold rolling-origin cross-validation and compare gradient boosting to two naïve baselines (WAPE = Σ|error| / Σ actual).

In [21]:
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit
H = 5
X = pd.DataFrame({"dis_l1": d.discharges, "dis_m7": d.discharges.rolling(7).mean(), "dis_m14": d.discharges.rolling(14).mean(),
                  "tr_m7": d.transfers.rolling(7).mean(), "in_m7": d.intake.rolling(7).mean(), "hhs": d.hhs_load, "cbp": d.cbp_load,
                  "dow": d.date.dt.dayofweek, "hhs_chg7": d.hhs_load.diff(7)})
y = d.discharges.shift(-H)
ok = X.notna().all(axis=1) & y.notna(); X, y = X[ok].reset_index(drop=True), y[ok].reset_index(drop=True)
wape = lambda a, p: float(np.abs(a - p).sum() / max(a.sum(), 1))
res = {"Last value": [], "7-day mean": [], "Gradient boosting": []}
for tr, te in TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5).split(X):
    res["Last value"].append(wape(y[te], X.dis_l1[te])); res["7-day mean"].append(wape(y[te], X.dis_m7[te]))
    mdl = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=200, max_depth=3, learning_rate=.05, random_state=0).fit(X.iloc[tr], y[tr])
    res["Gradient boosting"].append(wape(y[te], mdl.predict(X.iloc[te])))
out = pd.DataFrame(res).round(3); out.index = [f"fold {i+1}" for i in range(5)]; out.loc["mean"] = out.mean().round(3); out
Out[21]:
Last value 7-day mean Gradient boosting

fold 2 0.159 0.187 0.180
fold 3 0.190 0.194 0.172
fold 4 0.329 0.417 3.194
fold 5 0.421 0.360 0.401
mean 0.255 0.269 0.825

Finding (a negative result worth reporting). The simple last value baseline wins (≈ 26 % WAPE). Gradient boosting matches it in the three stable folds but fails badly (WAPE > 300 %) in the fold containing the early-2025 structural break, because tree models cannot extrapolate to a regime they have never seen. Short-term discharge volume is best tracked with simple persistence-based indicators plus change-detection alerts (as in the dashboard) rather than a black-box forecaster.

9. Summary of findings¶

  1. Transfers (CBP → HHS): ~78 % of CBP custody transferred per reporting day in 2023, ~76 % in 2024, but only ~50 % across 2025 and ~30 % by Q4 2025.
  2. Placements (HHS → sponsors): discharge effectiveness fell from 3.3 % / day (2023) to 2.9 % (2024) to 1.1 % (2025); in the four stagnation windows it was < 0.75 %.
  3. Delay: implied CBP dwell time exceeded the 72-hour benchmark (≈ 3.2–3.4 days) in H2 2025; implied HHS residence rose from ≈ 30 days to 150–230 days.
  4. Backlog: flow- and stock-based views disagree in 2023–24 (data-reconciliation gap) but agree in 2025, where the pipeline is slow-moving rather than overflowing.
  5. Pattern: discharges vary significantly by weekday (Tuesday weakest); transfer speed does not.
  6. Stability: outcome stability fell from ~77 to as low as ~6 in April 2025, after the early-2025 transition and has not returned to 2023–24 levels.
  7. Predictability: simple persistence beats gradient boosting, which breaks under the structural change.

All numbers above are reproducible by running this notebook top-to-bottom; the dashboard (app.py) exposes the same metrics interactively.
